title: CI/CD
description: Pipelines, automation and continuous delivery with GitHub Actions.
resumo: CI: merge to main at least daily, with build and tests on every push and pull request.
Continuous Delivery: always ready, a human approves production. Continuous Deployment: no approval, so monitoring and rollback are required.
Pipeline: checkout, build and tests, quality, image, staging, production — fastest checks first.
Use the Maven Wrapper in CI; tag images with the commit SHA, never only `latest`.
Quality gate: tests pass, coverage on new code, no critical vulnerabilities — and tests that really assert.
A red main is the first priority; `concurrency` keeps deploys in order.

subsections.subtitle: What Is CI/CD?
subsections.description: Automating the path from commit to production.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** without automation, integrations are rare and big, conflicts pile up, tests get skipped, and every manual deploy is a risky event.

**Concept:** CI (Continuous Integration) means integrating code into the main branch often, with an automatic build and tests on every change. CD means the software is always ready to release (Continuous Delivery) or is released automatically (Continuous Deployment). Both run in a pipeline: a scripted sequence of steps that every change goes through.

**How it works:** each change is small, checked the same way every time, and can go to production safely several times a day. The result is fast feedback and less risk per release.
examples.code:
commit -> push -> [CI: build + tests + quality] -> artifact (Docker image)
       -> [CD: deploy to staging -> tests -> approval?] -> production

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Having a pipeline but living with a red build. Every new commit lands on top of a failure, nobody knows which change broke what, and the pipeline stops protecting anything. A red main is the team's first priority: fix it or revert within minutes.
examples.code:
main: build FAILED 3 days ago — "it's just a flaky test"
every commit since then lands on a red build

RIGHT: fix or revert immediately; a red main blocks new merges

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a CI server alone is not CI. Branches that live for weeks still end in painful merges, even with a pipeline configured.

**Concept:** continuous integration means merging into the main branch at least daily, from short branches; an automatic build and tests on every change; a fast build (ideally under 10 minutes); and a broken build treated as the team's top priority.

**How it works:** run the pipeline on every push and every pull request, so problems show up before the merge, not after.
examples.code:
CI checklist:
[x] Every push and pull request runs the pipeline
[x] Reproducible build (Maven Wrapper, pinned versions)
[x] Automatic unit and integration tests
[x] Feedback in under 10 minutes
[x] main always green; a broken build is fixed right away
examples.interview_question: Which practices define real continuous integration?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Running CI only on main. Pull requests are not checked, so broken code is discovered after it was merged. Trigger on pull requests too.
examples.code:
# WRONG: PRs are not checked
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

# RIGHT
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** both are called "CD", but one has a human approval before production and the other does not — and that changes what the team needs.

**Concept:** in Continuous Delivery, every artifact that passes the pipeline is ready for production, but the final deploy waits for a manual approval — common with release windows or compliance rules. In Continuous Deployment there is no human step: everything that passes the tests goes straight to production.

**How it works:** continuous deployment needs very reliable tests, monitoring and automatic rollback, because nobody looks before it goes out.
examples.code:
Continuous Delivery:   CI -> staging (automatic) -> [manual approval] -> production
Continuous Deployment: CI -> staging (automatic) -> production (automatic, with rollback)
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Deploying automatically to production without alerts or automatic rollback. A bad change reaches every user, and nobody notices until customers complain. Add monitoring and a rollback path before removing the approval.
examples.code:
WRONG: tests pass -> production, nothing watching afterwards

RIGHT: tests pass -> production -> error rate and latency watched
       -> rollback automatically if they get worse

subsections.subtitle: Anatomy of a Pipeline
subsections.description: Stages, jobs, steps, runners and artifacts.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you need to read and change a pipeline at work, and the vocabulary — stages, jobs, runners, artifacts — gets in the way.

**Concept:** a pipeline is split into stages that run in sequence or in parallel: checkout, build and tests (`mvn verify`), quality and security analysis, building and publishing the Docker image, deploy to staging, smoke tests, promotion to production. Each stage runs on a runner (a machine or container) and passes artifacts along — the JAR or the image — instead of rebuilding them.

**How it works:** order the stages from fastest to slowest, so a typo fails in seconds rather than after twenty minutes of tests.
examples.code:
1. Checkout        actions/checkout
2. Build & tests   mvn -B verify (JDK 21)
3. Quality         coverage (JaCoCo), static analysis, dependency scan
4. Image           docker build + push to the registry (tag = commit SHA)
5. Staging         automatic deploy + smoke tests
6. Production      approval (delivery) or automatic (deployment)
examples.interview_question: What are the typical stages of a pipeline for a Spring Boot API?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Slow checks first. If the integration tests run before the compile and the linter, a missing semicolon costs twenty minutes. Fail fast: cheap checks first, independent ones in parallel.
examples.code:
WRONG:  integration tests (15 min) -> compile -> lint      -> typo found after 15 minutes
RIGHT:  compile + lint (1 min) -> unit tests -> integration tests

subsections.subtitle: GitHub Actions in Practice
subsections.description: A CI workflow for a Maven project.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** you want every push and pull request to build and test the project automatically, without a CI server to maintain.

**Concept:** workflows are YAML files in `.github/workflows`. The trigger (`on`) says when they run; each job runs on a runner, with steps executed in order. The `setup-java` action installs the JDK and caches the Maven repository, and `./mvnw -B verify` compiles, tests and runs the checks. Jobs can run in parallel and depend on each other with `needs`.

**How it works:** use the Maven Wrapper (`./mvnw`), so CI uses exactly the same Maven version as every developer.
examples.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: '21'
          cache: maven

      - name: Build and test
        run: ./mvnw -B verify
examples.interview_question: How do you set up a CI pipeline for a Maven project in GitHub Actions?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: `./mvnw: Permission denied`. The wrapper was committed from Windows without the executable bit, so it fails on the Linux runner. Mark it executable in Git.
examples.code:
# CI log
./mvnw: Permission denied
Error: Process completed with exit code 126.

# RIGHT
git update-index --chmod=+x mvnw
git commit -m "chore: make mvnw executable"

subsections.subtitle: Building the Image and the Registry

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** production runs an image tagged `latest`. Which code is that? Nobody knows, and rolling back to "the previous latest" is impossible.

**Concept:** tag every image with the commit SHA (or the semantic version for releases). That makes it immutable and traceable: you know exactly what runs in each environment. The same image is then promoted from staging to production without rebuilding.

**How it works:** the pipeline builds once and pushes to a registry — here, the GitHub Container Registry, using the workflow's own token.
examples.code:
docker:
  needs: build
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  permissions:
    contents: read
    packages: write
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
    - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
      with:
        push: true
        tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}
examples.interview_question: Why tag images with the commit SHA instead of "latest"?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Tagging with `latest` only. Each push overwrites the previous image, so there is nothing to roll back to and no way to tell environments apart.
examples.code:
# WRONG
tags: ghcr.io/shop/api:latest

# RIGHT: unique per commit (and a version tag for releases)
tags: |
  ghcr.io/shop/api:${{ github.sha }}
  ghcr.io/shop/api:1.4.0

subsections.subtitle: Tests and Quality Gates
subsections.description: Automatic criteria a change must meet before merging.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** code with failing tests, no tests at all, or a known vulnerability still gets merged, because nothing stops it.

**Concept:** a quality gate is a set of criteria the pipeline requires before a change can be merged: all tests pass, minimum coverage on new code, no critical bugs or vulnerabilities in static analysis, no serious CVEs in dependencies. If a criterion fails, the pull request cannot be merged.

**How it works:** focus the coverage rule on new code, so legacy projects are not blocked. JaCoCo can fail the build when coverage drops below a threshold.
examples.code:
<!-- pom.xml: fail the build if line coverage drops below 80% -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
  <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>0.8.12</version>
  <executions>
    <execution><goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals></execution>
    <execution>
      <id>check</id>
      <goals><goal>check</goal></goals>
      <configuration>
        <rules>
          <rule>
            <limits>
              <limit><counter>LINE</counter><value>COVEREDRATIO</value><minimum>0.80</minimum></limit>
            </limits>
          </rule>
        </rules>
      </configuration>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
examples.interview_question: What is a quality gate, and what should it check?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Chasing the coverage number with tests that assert nothing. Coverage only proves the code ran, not that its result was checked; the gate passes and bugs still get through. Review the assertions, not only the percentage (mutation testing, in the advanced level, measures this).

subsections.subtitle: Pipeline Best Practices
subsections.description: Fast, reliable and easy to maintain.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** a slow or flaky pipeline makes the team work around it: skipping checks, re-running until green, merging without waiting.

**Concept:** cache dependencies; run the fastest checks first (fail fast); run independent jobs in parallel; pin versions of actions and images; keep builds reproducible; use the same commands locally and in CI (Maven Wrapper); treat the pipeline as code, reviewed in pull requests.

**How it works:** `concurrency` cancels outdated runs of the same branch, so only the latest commit is built.
examples.code:
Fast pipeline:
  - cache ~/.m2 (setup-java cache: maven)
  - lint and unit tests before integration tests
  - parallel jobs: tests | static analysis | dependency scan
  - concurrency: cancel older runs of the same branch

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
examples.interview_question: Which practices make a CI/CD pipeline efficient?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Deploys without concurrency control. Two merges in a row start two deploys at the same time, and the older one may finish last, leaving production on the previous version. Queue deploys — and do not cancel one that is running.
examples.code:
# WRONG: two deploys can run in parallel

# RIGHT: one deploy at a time, the next one waits
concurrency:
  group: deploy-production
  cancel-in-progress: false
